sources.title: Christian Julien Robin and Paul Yule: Ẓafār
sources.note: Full indexed original Thematic Dictionary of Ancient Arabia, 2023, updated September 2024. Early epigraphic records, dhu-Raydān/Himyar, late antiquity and irrigation architecture. Direct page/DOI fetch failed; indexed full original read. Start 110 BCE is calendar-era epoch and possible secession, not a securely documented foundation.

sources.title: Jérémie Schiettecatte: Des royaumes combattants, first to third centuries
sources.note: Direct French Ministry of Culture archaeological account by the researcher. Highland centres, competing kingdoms, annexations around 275 and 300, Makhawan/Mocha port. Dates treated as approximate; no claim that modern Mocha coffee exports existed in antiquity.

sources.title: Jérémie Schiettecatte: Himyar, a monotheist kingdom expanding into Arabia
sources.note: Direct Ministry of Culture account, Le pouvoir du Himyar: annexations, northern expansion, Kinda intermediary. Religious uniformity in this short overview not adopted; Robin 2021 provides the more qualified religious assessment.

sources.title: Jérémie Schiettecatte: La domination éthiopienne
sources.note: Direct Ministry of Culture account: Yusuf persecution, Aksumite intervention, Abraha dam repairs and 548 diplomacy, Persian intervention and provincial rule circa575. Exact disputed reign bounds omitted. No adoption of source’s claim that conquest ended the whole civilization.

sources.title: Yule, Rösch and Fischer: The Highland Environment of Himyarite Zafar
sources.note: University-hosted author manuscript for 2010 conference. Full indexed original read; direct PDF and downloaded file return access challenge. Page 3 Irrigational technology and Sources for Himyarite Agriculture: terraces, water/soil retention, Himyarite-style reservoir masonry; al-Aḍlaʿ utilitarian ceramics. Modern field counts not projected into antiquity.

sources.title: Franke, Rösch, Ruppert and Yule: Zafar, Sixth Preliminary Report, February to March 2006
sources.note: Direct PDF downloaded from German National Library. Zeitschrift für Orient-Archäologie 1 (2008), pages 208 to 245. Selected Small Finds pp 220 to 221; Charred Plant Remains pp 221 to 223. PDF human pages 13 to 16. Covers excavated material, not reconstructed recipes; ambiguous mixed deposits not turned into a single dated meal.

sources.title: Peter Stein: Carved, Signed, Crossed Out, Documents on Wooden Sticks
sources.note: Direct author article, Ancient Near East Today 10.10, October 2022. Fig2 includes fifth-century L102; cursive correspondence, signatures, annulment, scribal exercises. Tradition predates Himyar and continued within its period; no universal schooling inferred.

sources.title: Christian Julien Robin: The Judaism of the Ancient Kingdom of Himyar in Arabia
sources.note: Direct openly published chapter downloaded and extracted locally; Diversity and Rabbinization (2021), pp165 to270. Printed 167 religious change 380 to 384 ;177 to 178 Garb Bayt al-Ashwal1 around 380 to 420 ;180 Ry520 January 465. Exact transcription mrʾ ḥyn w-mwtn and English Lord of life and of death visually checked on printed 178/human PDF 16. No reconstructed monumental glyphs.

sources.title: University of Basel: Research on droughts in sixth-century Arabia
sources.note: Direct 2022 report from research team, linking Science10.1126/science.abg4044. Oman cave proxy and other regional/historical evidence suggest drought contributed alongside conflict. Cave dating alone has thirty-year uncertainty; no claim climate caused Islam or uniquely caused Himyar’s decline.

sources.title: British Museum: Bronze anatomical votive, 1983,0626.2
sources.note: Full indexed original curatorial and Bowers catalogue entries. Second to third century; dedication by Wahab Ta’lab for well-being, cast leaded bronze, fingers downward, inscription added after casting. Bowers entry explicitly questions identification of its Zafar with the Himyarite capital; public prose treats this as regional context and states the distinction.

proposedOverrides.name: Himyarite Kingdom
proposedOverrides.summary: A highland South Arabian kingdom joining irrigated agriculture, regional conquest, maritime connections and a rich written record.

batchIdentityNotes.identity: Correct indexed spelling is himyarite-kingdom, not parent suggestion hymiarite-kingdom. No existing card or staged claim; no alias association.
batchIdentityNotes.dates: Index-1 to600 circa; BCE appearance predates map. Around275 Saba annexation, around300 Hadramawt; independent dynasty displaced525 or shortly after, later Abraha, Persian government circa575. Date-phase boundaries deliberately marked circa. No implied foundation in1BCE or precise fall600.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: world-bc1 throughworld400 repeat bbox[39.055,12.613,49.711,22.748]; world500[39.527,12.613,52.357,21.276]. Broad coastal/highland shape across different political configurations, publicly cautioned; no geometry fix.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Garb Bayt al-Ashwal1 around 380 to 420, mrʾ ḥyn w-mwtn, Sabaic Roman transcription and Lord of life and of death; Robin2021 printed177/178, humanPDF15/16. Downloaded original and visually checked page178.
batchIdentityNotes.scope: Wooden writing is explicitly older regional practice continuing into fifth century. Bronze hand explicitly not securely from Himyar capital. No invented schooling, medical efficacy or sanitation system. Main archaeological report mixes debris dates and collection/excavation finds, preserved in wording.
batchIdentityNotes.unused: Yemen2025 tentative UNESCO nomination was consulted but not used: chronology and assertions diverge from excavation literature. No UNESCO-inscribed status claimed.
